network.tdh.verify.metadataDescription: Every day, the Rust core, the Python reference and 6529.io’s TDH side by side: how many identity records agree, and every difference counted and classed by cause.

network.tdh.verify.title: TDH verification
network.tdh.verify.lede: Every day the Rust core and the Python reference compute every collector’s TDH, and both are compared with 6529.io’s published values. Differences are counted and classed by cause; no individual record is published.

network.tdh.verify.mode.unchecked: History read from Ethereum log servers, not yet fully checked. The snapshot block is linked header by header to a recent finalized block, and the edition floors are proven against it; the light client starts from the first beacon server’s checkpoint, with no pinned checkpoint yet. The history before the snapshot was read from public log servers and is taken as reported. It stays so, even once 6529’s own Ethereum node is synced, until the daily run checks the full history against that node. Nothing in these runs signs.

network.tdh.verify.calendar.heading: Every day

network.tdh.verify.side.heading: Side by side
network.tdh.verify.side.caption: The day’s results from each implementation. 6529.io’s values are the object under test.
network.tdh.verify.side.runtimeNote: The Rust core’s time is its whole run: reading Ethereum and checking what is checked today (the day’s headers, linked to a finalized block, and the proofs of the edition floors), then computing. The history before the snapshot is not yet checked. Computing alone takes the Rust reference, of which the Rust core is a copy, about 0.6 s (P52 §3.4). The Python reference’s time is its whole run on the Rust run’s input.
network.tdh.verify.side.rootsHelp: The cycle root binds the day, the snapshot block, the rule version with its registry hash, the wallet tree, each identity’s TDH per card, and the counts and total; validators will sign it. The wallet root is the tree of every wallet record outside the two sinks. The history root commits to every log of the four contracts from their deployment through the snapshot block, with its time and transaction; a new validator may take the history from the network when it matches the root that keys with more than two thirds of the weight report. Equal record files give equal roots.
network.tdh.verify.side.pythonRoots: None: its record files are compared byte for byte with Rust’s
network.tdh.verify.side.computedRust: Read from public Ethereum servers, then computed: the snapshot checked, the history as reported
network.tdh.verify.side.computedPython: Computed from the Rust run’s input, SHA-256 checked
network.tdh.verify.diff.heading: Differences
network.tdh.verify.diff.lede: A difference is any identity or wallet record that is not equal in every compared field, between the Rust core and the Python reference or between the Rust core and 6529.io. Each is counted once, with its class and its cause.
network.tdh.verify.diff.none: No differences: every compared field of every record is equal.
network.tdh.verify.diff.countsMissing: Records differ on this day, but its file carries no counts by class.
network.tdh.verify.diff.privacy: Individual records are never published, not even under a label: one differing token can single out its holder. The daily job keeps the per-record detail in a private report and publishes only these counts.
network.tdh.verify.diff.history: How it started: before transaction netting, the runs of October 14 and 15 had 10,280 of 10,282 identity records and 11,131 of 11,133 wallet records equal, with totals 240 TDH below 6529.io’s. DEV-2, the order of transfers, has two cases. Both differences were the first: a token sent out and back within one transaction, which D131’s netting settled; the reruns of those two days are equal everywhere. The second, a sale and a purchase in different transactions of one block, can still differ until the cutover.
network.tdh.verify.class.A.body: Against 6529.io: a known, deliberate difference between TDH-v1 and the old backend (a DEV item).
network.tdh.verify.class.B.body: Against 6529.io: a known issue in the old backend (a BUG item).
network.tdh.verify.class.C.body: The Rust core and the Python reference disagree: a defect in one of the two new programs.
network.tdh.verify.class.D.body: Against 6529.io, with no known cause. Every difference from 6529.io is class D until it is matched to a known one, and it raises an alarm.
network.tdh.verify.class.note: Class A and B differences are explained, not accepted: the owner still decides what to do with each. Since D131’s netting the list of known differences is empty, so any difference from 6529.io raises an alarm.

network.tdh.verify.provenance.heading: Provenance
network.tdh.verify.provenance.remote: 6529’s public TDH feed, served from 6529’s CloudFront address d379duzqnomz3w.cloudfront.net: the daily job’s published files, linked below. The job runs once a day at 00:40 UTC and fetches a late 6529.io file again at 06:00 and 12:00 UTC. This page rechecks the index and the latest day every 10 minutes, and older days every hour. The feed’s index states a SHA-256 for each day’s file; this page recomputes it from the bytes it read and shows whether the two match. Neither is a signature.
network.tdh.verify.provenance.ruleFromSp: TDH-v1, rule version tdh-v1.0. This day’s file does not state its rule version; this is the specification’s.
network.tdh.verify.provenance.registryFr: The specification’s hash for tdh-v1.0; not stated in this day’s file.
network.tdh.verify.provenance.commitsNot: Neither repository is public: the validator’s is to be published when the owner decides (D116), and the Python reference is in 6529’s private design repository. Each run records its commits, so it can be reproduced from them.

network.tdh.verify.provenance.filesNote: Files, by SHA-256: the canonical input the Rust core read and the Python reference computed from, and the identity and wallet record files each wrote. Equal hashes mean byte-identical files, so a later run of the published source on the same input can be checked against them.

network.tdh.verify.check.heading: Check it yourself
network.tdh.verify.check.intro: What anyone can check today, what that does not reach, and how a day is reproduced with the source code.
network.tdh.verify.check.upload: 6529.io’s own public API lists every day’s upload with its block and a link to its file on Arweave. Open the day’s file from that list and check on Arweave that its signer is 6529.io’s upload key:
network.tdh.verify.check.block: Open the snapshot block on a block explorer: it is the last block before 00:00 UTC of the day.
network.tdh.verify.check.file: Download the day’s JSON above: every number on this page comes from it.
network.tdh.verify.check.limit: None of this reaches the Rust or Python numbers: checking them needs their source code, which is not public. The validator’s, with the Rust core and the daily tools, is to be published when the owner decides (D116); the Python reference is in 6529’s private design repository.
network.tdh.verify.check.sourceBody: A day’s run is three commands, from the validator repository with a checkout of 6529’s design repository beside it, which holds the Python reference. The Rust run reads Ethereum and writes its canonical input; the Python reference computes from that input after checking its SHA-256; the three-way comparison fetches 6529.io’s files, verifies them and compares every record:
network.tdh.verify.check.compare: Then compare: your cycle root and wallet root must equal the ones on this page, and your identities.jsonl and wallets.jsonl must equal your own Python run’s byte for byte, with the SHA-256 that Provenance gives for each file when the day’s file states them.
network.tdh.verify.method.heading: How this works
network.tdh.verify.method.snapshot.title: The same snapshot.
network.tdh.verify.method.snapshot.body: All three use the snapshot block of the day, the last Ethereum block before 00:00 UTC.
network.tdh.verify.method.inputs.title: Independent computation.
network.tdh.verify.method.inputs.body: The Rust core reads the day’s events from Ethereum and computes TDH-v1. The Python reference computes from the same input, after checking its SHA-256, so the two compare computation, not reading Ethereum. 6529.io’s values come from the files it publishes every day on Arweave, accepted only when the upload key’s signature and the file’s size and data root verify. 6529.io’s values are the object under test, never an input.
network.tdh.verify.method.exact.title: Exact comparison.
network.tdh.verify.method.exact.body: The TDH fields of every collector and wallet are compared for exact equality, with no tolerance. In 6529.io’s column names: each record’s boost, boosted TDH (final TDH), TDH (base TDH) and unweighted days (raw days); the same three TDH values for each collection; and for every token its balance, rate, TDH and unweighted days. Record counts, totals and the snapshot block are compared too. The upload’s other columns (ranks, balance and set counts, BUG-15, and display names) are not written by these runs and are not compared.
network.tdh.verify.method.classes.title: Classification.
network.tdh.verify.method.classes.body: Each differing record is classed A to D. A difference between the Rust core and the Python reference is class C. A difference from 6529.io is explained, as class A or B, only when it is on the list of known ones; any other is class D. Classes C and D both raise an alarm.
network.tdh.verify.method.after.title: After the cutover,
network.tdh.verify.method.after.body: 6529.io runs the Rust core, so their agreement shows that what is published is what was computed. The Python reference stays the independent check of the computation.
network.tdh.verify.method.validators: Once validators run, P53 requires each to sign before it reads 6529.io’s values, so those values cannot influence its vote.
network.tdh.verify.flow.title: The daily comparison
network.tdh.verify.flow.desc: Two flows meet in the comparison. Ethereum feeds the Rust core, and the Python reference computes from the Rust run’s input. Separately, 6529.io’s backend publishes its upload on Arweave. The comparison publishes the files this page reads.
network.tdh.verify.flow.sameCode: After the cutover, the 6529.io backend runs the same Rust core.
network.tdh.verify.flow.text: Ethereum → Rust core. The Rust run’s input, SHA-256 checked → Python reference. Both → Compare. 6529.io backend → Arweave upload → Compare. Compare → published JSON → this page. After the cutover, the 6529.io backend runs the Rust core.

network.tdh.verify.class.expectedDev2: A sale and a purchase of one card in different transactions of one block. TDH-v1 keeps their on-chain order (DEV-2) and the old backend does not, so a few wallets’ TDH could differ until the cutover (D132). It is not on the list of known differences: it would show here as class D, not yet explained, and raise an alarm until 6529 matches it to DEV-2. From the cutover, 6529.io shows the Rust core’s value.
